hook: Mr. Reyes, 71, takes warfarin to prevent clots from forming in his heart, which beats irregularly. A week after starting an antibiotic, he notices large bruises and pink urine. His INR, normally kept between 2 and 3, is 6.5. His doctor stops the warfarin and gives vitamin K. To see why a vitamin reverses a blood thinner, and why his clotting test now runs several times longer than normal, you need to know how clotting works.

prereq.q: In a positive feedback loop, what does the response do?
options: It keeps the variable at a set point
prereq.why: Positive feedback amplifies: the response strengthens the stimulus that produced it, until some outside event ends the loop.

prereq.q: Which plasma protein is converted into the threads of a clot?
prereq.why: Fibrinogen, made by the liver, is the clotting protein that forms the threads of a clot. Serum lacks it because the clot used it up.

options: A fragment of a megakaryocyte, with no nucleus
A small white blood cell with a round nucleus
prereq.why: Platelets are nucleus-free fragments broken off megakaryocytes in the marrow. They live 7–10 days.

chain.cause: A vessel wall is torn, exposing collagen and the tissue factor on cells outside the lining.
chain.effect: The smooth muscle of the wall contracts (vascular spasm), slowing the flow through the vessel.

chain.cause: Slower blood meets exposed collagen coated with von Willebrand factor.
chain.effect: Platelets adhere, activate, release ADP and thromboxane A2, and recruit more platelets into a soft plug.

chain.cause: Tissue factor binds factor VIIa and activates factors X and IX.
chain.effect: Factor Xa, with Va, makes a small amount of thrombin (initiation).

chain.cause: The small amount of thrombin activates the platelets in the plug and factors V, VIII and XI.
chain.effect: The activated platelet surface hosts IXa–VIIIa and Xa–Va, which make a burst of thrombin (amplification, then propagation).

chain.cause: The burst of thrombin cuts fibrinogen into fibrin and activates factor XIII.
chain.effect: Cross-linked fibrin threads bind the plug into a firm clot that seals the tear.

ideas: Hemostasis (hemo- = blood, -stasis = standing still) is the stopping of bleeding from a damaged vessel. It is not the same as clotting: it has three overlapping steps, vascular spasm, the platelet plug and coagulation, and clotting is only the third.

Fibrinolysis (fibrin + -lysis = breaking down) is the breakdown of fibrin once the wall is repaired. Plasminogen and tissue plasminogen activator both bind fibrin in the clot, and there tPA converts plasminogen into the enzyme plasmin, which cuts the fibrin into fragments so the clot dissolves over days.

Two drugs slow coagulation. Heparin binds antithrombin and makes it inactivate thrombin and factor Xa about a thousand times faster, working within minutes. Warfarin blocks the liver enzyme that recycles vitamin K, so clotting factors II, VII, IX and X are made in a non-working form, and it takes 3 to 5 days to act.

Hemophilia (-philia = tendency) is an inherited lack of a clotting factor, factor VIII in hemophilia A and factor IX in hemophilia B. The genes lie on the X chromosome, so males with one faulty copy have the disease. Without those factors the burst of thrombin on platelets cannot form.

A thrombus (Greek = clot) is a clot that forms inside an unbroken vessel and stays attached to its wall; in an artery it can block flow to the tissue beyond. A piece that breaks off and travels in the blood is an embolus, and the blockage where it lodges is an embolism.

Thrombocytopenia (-penia = shortage) is a platelet count below about 150,000 per microliter. Too few platelets cause bleeding from small vessels in the skin and mucous membranes, such as pinpoint red spots and bleeding gums, while a clotting factor problem causes deep bleeding into joints and muscles.

misconception.wrong: In the body, the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways are two separate routes, and either one alone can make a clot.
misconception.right: The two pathways describe what happens in test tubes, and they are still how the PT and aPTT are read. In the body, clotting starts when tissue factor is exposed, makes a little thrombin, and then depends on factors VIII and IX to make the burst of thrombin on activated platelets. That is why people with hemophilia bleed even though tissue factor and factor VII work normally, and why people who lack factor XII do not bleed abnormally.

summary: Hemostasis stops bleeding in three overlapping steps. Vascular spasm narrows the injured vessel. A platelet plug forms as platelets adhere to exposed collagen through von Willebrand factor, activate, release ADP and thromboxane A2, and aggregate through fibrinogen bridges. Coagulation turns the plug into a firm clot: in the cell-based model, tissue factor and factor VIIa make a little thrombin (initiation), that thrombin activates platelets and factors V, VIII and XI (amplification), and IXa–VIIIa and Xa–Va on the platelet surface make a burst of thrombin that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, cross-linked by XIIIa (propagation). Thrombin's positive feedback is confined by flow, healthy lining and antithrombin. The lab model's extrinsic (PT/INR) and intrinsic (aPTT) pathways meet at factor X and the common pathway. Vitamin K is needed to make factors II, VII, IX and X. Clots retract as platelets pull on fibrin, and fibrinolysis by plasmin, made from plasminogen by tPA, removes them. Heparin boosts antithrombin; warfarin blocks vitamin K recycling; aspirin blocks platelet thromboxane. Too little clotting (thrombocytopenia, hemophilia) causes bleeding; too much causes a thrombus, which can break off as an embolus.
